job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Daria Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Daria, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my grandmother and my aunt Rosa in a third-floor flat in Alderbrook. I wake early because Abuela likes breakfast at seven, and then I do the shopping and check the job boards on my old laptop. On Saturdays and Sundays I work at the garden centre by the ring road, lifting bags of compost and running the till. I studied business administration and passed, with no internship, and for six months I've been sending applications for office assistant and junior accounts jobs. I like routine, so I'm trying to find a steady office where I'd know what to do on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, nothing changes, and I'd be glad. I don't talk about it much with friends because most of them don't care. I'd tell my aunt it's like every other big claim, loud for a year and then forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still worried. No AI change doesn't make a job appear. I have a pass degree, a small debt, and a cushion of two months of savings. That's what keeps me up, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working weekends at the garden centre and do more applications, around ten a week, with a better CV. I'd ask the manager if there's an admin role in the office there, since I already know the staff. I'd also go to the job centre's drop-in on Wednesdays and ask my uncle's friend at the logistics firm if he has anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but with a small knot in my stomach. It's like waiting for a letter from the council that never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your ideal first office job look like on a Monday morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A desk, a clear list of tasks, a manager who tells me what's expected, and a lunch break at the same time. I'm not asking for fancy. I'd like to be good at something quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think of people who say they use AI tools every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think good for them, I guess. I'm not against it, I just don't trust things that change every month. I'd rather learn one thing properly than ten things badly.

say: I'd say nothing changes and I'm **glad**, because it's like every other loud claim.
I rarely talk about it with **friends** since most don't care.
think: No AI change doesn't make a **job** appear, and a pass degree is my real problem.
Two months of **savings** and a small debt keep me awake, not machines.
do: Send **ten applications** a week and ask the garden centre manager about an office role.
Go to the job centre's Wednesday **drop-in** and ask my uncle's friend at the logistics firm.
feel: Steady, with a small **knot** in my stomach, like waiting for a letter.
S0.quote: No AI change doesn't make a job appear.
fieldNote: She is **anxious** from debt and no offer, not from AI.
She wants routine and calls herself resistant to constant change.
Weekend work gives her a small income and local contacts.

steps.text: Send ten applications a week with an improved CV
Keep working weekends at the garden centre
Ask my uncle's friend at the logistics firm about a vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough for people starting out. I'd tell friends to keep their options open and not to bank everything on one job. If someone asks me online, I'd say wait to see which jobs really change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. Office assistant jobs are mostly writing emails, booking and filing, which is what the card says goes first. The jobs I'm applying for might be the ones that shrink, and I never learned any of the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to try the tools, even though I don't like it. My aunt would show me on her phone, and I'd practise at night. I'd widen my search to customer-facing work and the council, since they hire slowly but steadily. I'd also stop buying lunch out and put the money in Abuela's savings jar for the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. I feel like I'm being told to run when I haven't learned to walk. But I'd do it, because I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of an office assistant's day would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emails, filing, booking appointments, and entering invoices. That's exactly the first six months of an office job, the part where you prove yourself. If software does that, the entry route is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be willing to try the tools if a firm required it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes. I'd tell them I'm a slow starter but I'm careful, and I don't make the same mistake twice. I think that counts for something.

say: I'd say it's rough for people **starting out** and tell friends not to bank on one job.
Online I'd say wait and see which jobs really **change**.
think: Office assistant work is mostly emails, booking and **filing**, which goes first.
I never learned the **tools**, so I'm scared.
do: Let my aunt show me the tools on her **phone** and practise at night.
Widen my search to **customer-facing** work and the council, and skip lunches out.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, like told to run before I've learned to walk.
S1.quote: I'm a slow starter but I'm careful, and I don't make the same mistake twice.
fieldNote: Her fear is concrete: the **entry-level tasks** she applies for are the ones AI takes.
She will learn the tools only when pushed, and she knows it.
She trades quickness for carefulness as a selling point.

steps.text: Practise the tools on my aunt's phone at night
Apply to customer-facing roles and council jobs
Stop buying lunch out and save the money for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to act now. I'm not usually political, but two years isn't time for anyone to cope. I'd tell friends to talk to their families and to save what they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. The kind of work I trained for would be done by AI before I've had a real first job. I'd be twenty-five with a pass degree, no experience and nothing the machines can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every hour I can at the garden centre, since robots for hands-on work come later. I'd cut every cost, move my savings into the safest account and ask my aunt Rosa about her salon, in case I can learn to do the books or the front desk. I'd also go to the council and ask what support exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic. A quiet one, the kind where I stay very still and think too much. I'd lie awake counting money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Abuela it's a storm, and we just need to sit tight. She lived through hard times and she'd say we'll manage. But I'd see her worry about me, and that would be the hardest part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the garden centre was your only income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to move to a full-time shift and maybe earn enough to cover my share of the rent. It's not a career, but it's hands and a pay slip. I'd feel lucky to have it.

say: I'd say the government has to act now since two years is **not enough** time.
I'd tell friends to talk to their families and **save**.
think: My trained kind of work could be done by AI before my first real **job**.
I'd be twenty-five with a pass degree and **no experience**.
do: Take every hour at the **garden centre**, since hands-on work is reached later.
Move savings into the safest account and ask my aunt about her **salon** books.
feel: Quiet **panic**, the still kind where I think too much.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-five with a pass degree, no experience and nothing the machines can't do.
fieldNote: The **two-year** window leaves her with no experience and no time to gain it.
She turns to family and hands-on weekend work as a fallback.
Her worry about her grandmother worrying is as strong as her own fear.

steps.text: Move to full-time hours at the garden centre
Put savings into the safest account available
Ask the council what support exists for young jobseekers
Cut every cost that isn't rent, food or travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's something. I'd tell friends to make a plan and not wait. I'd probably support more training in schools and colleges, since that's what's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel a bit better, but not safe. I could get a first job and a little experience before it lands. Still, I'm slow to learn new tools, and I'd be racing the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any office job that gets me inside a company, even part time, and learn what the firm does and who does what. I'd learn the AI tools there, not alone at night, because people around me would help. I'd save a quarter of my pay and keep the weekend job for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. A plan makes the worry smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More time to learn slowly. If I get a job this year, I'd have four years to learn the tools properly, on the job, with people showing me. That works better for me than two weeks of panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be preparing people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Schools, colleges and employers, I think. And the government, a bit. I'm not angry at anyone, I just think no single person can prepare for this alone.

say: I'd say five years isn't long but it's **something**, so make a plan.
I'd support more **training** in schools and colleges.
think: I feel a bit better but not safe, because I'm slow to learn **new tools**.
do: Take any **office job**, even part time, and learn the AI tools there with colleagues.
Save a **quarter** of my pay and keep the weekend job.
feel: Worried, but a **plan** makes the worry smaller.
S3.quote: I'm not angry at anyone, I just think no single person can prepare for this alone.
fieldNote: She remains **anxious** because her slow learning style is up against a clock.
She wants to learn on the job with people, not alone.
She does not blame anyone, which fits her centre view.

steps.text: Take any office job and learn the firm's software with colleagues
Learn the AI tools on the job with people showing me
Save a quarter of every pay cheque
Keep the weekend garden centre shifts for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no need to panic. I'd tell friends to get a job, learn along the way and keep an eye on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly okay. I could have a job, some seniority and a few good habits by then. I'd still worry a bit, because slow learners are the last to be picked for new roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find a steady office job, learn the firm properly, and then slowly add a skill each year, like spreadsheets or data entry tools. I'd save for a small flat and keep my aunt and grandmother close. I'd also aim for a role where I deal with people, not only screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little hollow. I know ten years can still turn into one fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you feel calmer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere settled, with a small team, maybe a supervisor. Not rich, not famous, just known as the person who knows how things work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhat, yes. Ten years lets me earn trust at a company before anything big changes. That's the thing I'm best at.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so no need to panic.
I'd tell friends to get a job and **learn** along the way.
think: I'm fairly okay, with a job and some **seniority** by then.
Slow learners are the **last** picked for new roles.
do: Find a steady **office job** and add one skill a year, like spreadsheets.
Save for a small **flat** and aim for a people-facing role.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me earn trust at a company before anything big changes.
fieldNote: A **decade** helps her most, but she remains anxious because the first job is still missing.
She values trust and routine over speed.
She knows slow learners get picked last.

steps.text: Find a steady office job and learn the firm properly
Add one new software skill each year
Save for a small flat near my family
Stay close to Abuela and aunt Rosa and share rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's too fast for a slow learner like me. What would help is a proper first job with training built in, and someone patient to show me the tools without making me feel stupid. Money for the rent while I learn would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that quiet people get missed. We don't say much, but we're here, and we work hard. I'd like firms to notice that.

headlineQuote: Quiet people get missed. We don't say much, but we're here, and we work hard.
portrait: Daria is a 23-year-old business administration graduate living with her **grandmother and aunt** in Alderbrook.
She passed with no internship, has some debt and works **weekends** at a garden centre.
She is centrist and resistant: she likes routine, never uses AI and is **slow** to pick up tools.
She is anxious even in the mild picture and **alarmed** at the 2-year warning.
Her fallbacks are the weekend job, her aunt's salon and a very close family.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028**, because it is too fast for someone who learns slowly.
whatWouldHelp: A first job with **training** built in and a patient person to teach her the tools.
